intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, language delay, and skeletal defects with or without seizures (NEDHLSS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CACNA1C gene (114205) on chromosome 12p13.33.

paragraphs.text: Bozarth et al. (2018) described a girl (patient 1) of English/Ukrainian ancestry, born to nonconsanguineous parents, who had neonatal-onset epileptic encephalopathy. Tonic and tonic-myoclonic seizures began within hours of birth and evolved into epileptic tonic spasms at 3 months of age. Multiple antiepileptic drugs failed to control the seizures, although clobazam reduced them. She had profound axial and appendicular hypotonia, no developmental progress at 18 months, inability to fixate or track visually, and severe sleep-wake disturbance. Other features were laryngomalacia, bilateral clubfeet, 3-4 finger and 2-3 toe syndactyly, camptodactyly, micrognathia, downturned corners of the mouth, frontal bossing, scant hair, inverted nipples, mild optic nerve hypoplasia, anal stenosis, and dysphagia requiring a gastrostomy tube. EEG showed distinctive diffuse excessive fast activity. Brain MRI, echocardiogram, and Holter monitoring were normal.

paragraphs.text: Bozarth et al. (2018) also described a family of Irish and German descent. The proband (patient 2), a girl, had tetralogy of Fallot, which was repaired at 2 months of age. At 4 months she developed severe biventricular failure with left ventricular noncompaction. She had mild dysmorphic features, including flat nasal bridge, low-set cupped ears, deep-set eyes, thin upper lip, and round face. She also had mild 2-3-4 toe syndactyly, mild developmental delay, and mild hypotonia. Her father (patient 3) had a congenital ventricular septal defect, aortic valve stenosis, learning disabilities, and ADHD. He developed focal-to-generalized tonic-clonic seizures at age 18 years, and his craniofacial features were similar to his daughter's. Bozarth et al. (2018) noted that seizures had rarely been reported in CACNA1C-related disorders, with only 3 individuals reported before their series. They concluded that their findings extended the phenotype to neonatal-onset epileptic encephalopathy and late-onset epilepsy, and that this family showed variable expressivity. They suggested including CACNA1C on epilepsy gene panels.

paragraphs.text: Rodan et al. (2021) reported 25 individuals from 22 families with heterozygous CACNA1C variants. Fourteen individuals had de novo nontruncating variants, and all of them had developmental delay or intellectual disability. At last follow-up, 9 were nonverbal and 6 were nonambulatory. One had a formal diagnosis of autism and 6 others had autistic features. Twelve were hypotonic and 4 had ataxia. Prenatal findings included reduced fetal movement (3 of 14), bilateral clubfoot (2 of 14), and oligohydramnios (2 of 14). The course was consistent with a static neurodevelopmental disorder. Brain MRI was normal except for an incidental arachnoid cyst in 1 individual and prominent cerebellar folia in another. Ten of the 14 had epilepsy, with onset between 2 months and 8 years. Both generalized and focal epilepsies occurred, including West syndrome/infantile spasms, myoclonic seizures, and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Seizures were fever-sensitive in 3 individuals and medically refractory in 4, and EEG findings were not consistent across the group. Twelve of the 14 had orthopedic abnormalities. Two had bilateral clubfoot with congenital finger contractures and 2 others had persistently adducted thumbs. Other orthopedic findings were kyphosis or scoliosis (2 of 14), congenital hip dysplasia (3 of 14), syndactyly (2 of 14), and joint hypermobility (3 of 14). Nine of 11 individuals with nontruncating variants who had ECGs had normal results. One individual (P13) had prolonged QT with T-wave alternans on Holter monitoring, and another had a possible ventricular conduction delay. Echocardiograms showed only minor findings, and no individual had the physical features of Timothy syndrome.

paragraphs.text: The evidence supports autosomal dominant transmission of NEDHLSS. Most reported heterozygous CACNA1C mutations occurred de novo (Kosaki et al., 2018; Bozarth et al., 2018; Rodan et al., 2021). Bozarth et al. (2018) reported transmission of a CACNA1C splice site variant from an affected father to his affected daughter. Rodan et al. (2021) found that 3 truncating variants were paternally inherited and segregated with neurodevelopmental abnormalities in the families. Penetrance and expressivity appeared variable among family members with truncating variants.

paragraphs.text: Rodan et al. (2021) identified heterozygous CACNA1C variants in 25 individuals from 22 families who were ascertained through GeneMatcher and ClinVar. The variants were found by exome sequencing or an intellectual disability gene panel. Thirteen unrelated individuals had missense variants, 1 had an in-frame deletion, and 11 individuals from 8 families had predicted truncating variants. All nontruncating variants occurred de novo, as did all but 3 of the truncating variants. None of the variants were present in gnomAD, 1000 Genomes, or the Exome Variant Server. All missense variants affected highly conserved positions and were predicted to be damaging. The missense variants clustered in a linker segment of domain II (exon 13) and in domain IV (exon 35). The de novo nontruncating variants were F166L, K177R, R324W, V403M, L601R, M611T, L614P, L614R, L657F, I743del, V1187A, L1408V, and V1411L; V1411L was found in 2 unrelated patients. The de novo truncating variants were Q80fs, V996fs, R1377fs, and L1518fs. The paternally inherited truncating variants were R161X, W528X, and R1989X. A splice variant, c.2663+1G-C, was not inherited from the father. All truncating variants except 1, which lies in the last exon (exon 45), were predicted to undergo nonsense-mediated decay.

paragraphs.text: Rodan et al. (2021) identified de novo heterozygous mutations at codon val1411 of the CACNA1C gene, each resulting in a val1411-to-leu (V1411L) substitution, in 2 unrelated patients. P13 carried a c.4231G-C transversion. This patient had severe intellectual disability, infantile spasms that evolved to Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and prolonged QT with T-wave alternans on Holter monitoring. P14 carried a c.4231G-T transversion. P14 was an infant with severe global developmental delay, generalized epilepsy beginning at 2 months of age, hip dysplasia, syndactyly, and adducted thumbs.
